title: The Herods and the Roman Governors
summary: The Herodian family from Herod the Great to Agrippa II, the Roman prefects and procurators of Judea, the high priests they appointed, and the emperors above them, with dates and where each appears in the New Testament.

sections.body:
A first-time reader of the New Testament meets a King Herod who hunts the infant Jesus, a Herod who beheads John the Baptist and mocks Jesus before his crucifixion, a King Herod who kills the apostle James and is struck down at Caesarea, and a King Agrippa who listens to Paul and says he is nearly persuaded. These are four different men across three generations of one family. Alongside them stand Roman governors: Pilate, who condemns Jesus, and Felix and Festus, who keep Paul in custody for years. Knowing who these people were, and when they ruled, clears up a good deal of confusion and shows how carefully the Gospels and Acts are set in real time.

Luke is especially deliberate about this. He dates the start of John the Baptist's preaching with a list of six rulers: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene,” followed by the high priests Annas and Caiaphas (Luke 3:1-2). Every name in that list is known from other sources. The fifteenth year of Tiberius is usually reckoned as AD 28 or 29, though some count from an earlier co-regency with Augustus and arrive at 26 or 27. Lysanias was once thought to be a mistake, since the only well-known Lysanias died in 36 BC, but two inscriptions from Abila, datable between AD 14 and 29, name a later Lysanias as tetrarch.

Our main outside source for all of these rulers is Flavius Josephus, a Jewish priest and general who went over to the Romans in the war of AD 66 to 70 and wrote The Jewish War (in the 70s) and Jewish Antiquities (about AD 93 or 94) in Rome. Josephus had his own loyalties, to the Flavian emperors who were his patrons and to the Herodian king Agrippa II, whom he knew, but his accounts are detailed and often confirmed by coins and inscriptions. The Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria and the Roman historian Tacitus add a little more.

Herod was a family name. The founder, Herod the Great, passed it to several sons and grandsons, and the Gospels and Acts often use it as a title, as later writers might say ‘Caesar’. Mark even calls Antipas ‘King Herod’ (Mark 6:14), though Rome never let him hold that title; Matthew and Luke, more precisely, call him tetrarch, a ‘ruler of a quarter’ used loosely for a minor prince.

Herod was not by birth a Jew of the old stock. His father Antipater was an Idumean, from the Edomite people whom the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus had conquered and forcibly converted to Judaism late in the second century BC, and his mother was a Nabatean Arab. Antipater made himself indispensable to Rome during the civil wars of the Roman Republic, and his sons rose with him. When the Parthians invaded in 40 BC and set up the last Hasmonean, Antigonus, as king, Herod fled to Rome, where the Senate named him king of Judea. He needed three years and a Roman army to take his kingdom; Jerusalem fell to him in 37 BC. He married Mariamme, a Hasmonean princess, to give his throne legitimacy.

Herod ruled as a client king, free in his own realm so long as he kept order and kept faith with Rome. He survived the fall of his patron Mark Antony by persuading Octavian (soon to be Augustus) of his loyalty after the battle of Actium in 31 BC. He was one of the great builders of the ancient world. He founded the port city of Caesarea Maritima with an artificial harbor, rebuilt Samaria as Sebaste in Augustus's honor, and built the desert fortresses of Masada and Herodium, where his tomb was identified by Ehud Netzer in 2007. Above all, he rebuilt the temple in Jerusalem on a vast scale. Josephus dates the start of the work to Herod's eighteenth year (Antiquities 15.380), about 20 or 19 BC; the main sanctuary was finished quickly, but work on the courts went on for decades, which is why people could say to Jesus “This temple took forty-six years to build” (John 2:20), putting that conversation around AD 27 or 28.

Herod was also suspicious to the point of savagery toward anyone who might threaten his throne. He had his wife Mariamme executed in 29 BC, her two sons Alexander and Aristobulus strangled in 7 BC, and his eldest son Antipater killed only days before his own death. Josephus says he ordered that leading men be held in the hippodrome at Jericho and killed when he died, so that there would be mourning at his funeral (the order was not carried out). The killing of the infants of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16-18) is not recorded outside Matthew, and some historians doubt it for that reason; others reply that the death of perhaps a dozen or so children in a small village would hardly register in a reign of such violence, and that the story fits what is known of him.

Herod's death is usually dated to 4 BC, following Emil Schürer's classic history of the period. Josephus says Herod died after an eclipse of the moon and before a Passover, and reigned thirty-seven years from his appointment in Rome and thirty-four from the capture of Jerusalem (Antiquities 17.167, 191); the eclipse of 13 March 4 BC fits. W. E. Filmer (Journal of Theological Studies, 1966) argued for early 1 BC instead, pointing to the total eclipse of January 1 BC, and later defenders of that date, including David Beyer and Andrew Steinmann, have added evidence from older manuscripts and printed editions of Josephus that give a different figure for the reign of Herod's son Philip. The majority of historians still hold to 4 BC. Since Jesus was born before Herod died (Matthew 2:1; Luke 1:5), most scholars place his birth between about 6 and 4 BC; those who accept the later death date place it around 3 or 2 BC. The odd result that Jesus was born ‘before Christ’ comes from a sixth-century monk, Dionysius Exiguus, who miscalculated the year when he set up the AD system.

sections.h: Herod's sons: Archelaus, Antipas, and Philip
sections.body:
Herod's final will divided his kingdom among three sons, and Augustus confirmed it with changes. None of them received the title king. Archelaus became ethnarch (‘ruler of a people’) of Judea, Samaria, and Idumea; Antipas became tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, the land east of the Jordan; and Philip became tetrarch of the regions northeast of the Sea of Galilee.

Archelaus began badly, with a massacre of worshipers at the temple during his first Passover, and went on as he began. When Joseph returned from Egypt and learned “that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there” and settled in Galilee (Matthew 2:22). Archelaus sailed to Rome to have his inheritance confirmed while a Jewish embassy followed to protest against him, an episode many commentators hear behind Jesus' parable of the nobleman who “went to a distant country to lay claim to his kingship and then return” while his citizens sent word that they did not want him (Luke 19:12-14). In AD 6, after complaints from both Jews and Samaritans, Augustus deposed him and banished him to Vienne in Gaul. Judea then came under direct Roman rule.

Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea for more than forty years, from 4 BC to AD 39, through the whole of Jesus' ministry. He rebuilt Sepphoris, four miles from Nazareth, and founded a new capital, Tiberias, on the Sea of Galilee around AD 20. He divorced his first wife, a daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas IV, to marry Herodias, the wife of his half-brother. John the Baptist condemned the marriage, and Antipas imprisoned and executed him. Josephus tells the same story from a different angle (Antiquities 18.116-119): he places John's death at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, says Antipas feared John's influence with the crowds, and reports that many Jews saw Antipas's later defeat by Aretas as God's punishment for killing John. Jesus called Antipas “that fox” (Luke 13:32), and Luke alone records that Pilate sent Jesus to him during the trial (Luke 23:6-12). In AD 39 Antipas asked the emperor Caligula for the title of king; his nephew Agrippa accused him of stockpiling weapons, and Caligula exiled him to Gaul.

Philip, the quietest of the three, ruled a mostly non-Jewish territory (Gaulanitis, Trachonitis, Batanea, and parts of Ituraea) from 4 BC until his death in AD 33 or 34. He rebuilt Paneas as Caesarea Philippi, where Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ (Matthew 16:13-16), and raised Bethsaida to a city named Julias. He married Salome, the daughter of Herodias. Mark 6:17 calls Herodias the wife of ‘Philip’, while Josephus says her first husband was another Herod, a son of Herod the Great by a different wife; either this half-brother also bore the name Philip, as some suggest, or the Gospel tradition confused the two, as others conclude.

sections.h: Agrippa I, Agrippa II, and the women of the family
sections.body:
Herod Agrippa I, a grandson of Herod the Great through the executed Aristobulus, was raised in Rome among the imperial family and was a friend of Caligula. When Caligula became emperor in AD 37 he gave Agrippa Philip's former territory with the title of king; in 39 or 40 he added the territory of the exiled Antipas; and in 41 Claudius, whose accession Agrippa had helped secure, gave him Judea and Samaria as well. For three years Agrippa ruled a kingdom nearly as large as his grandfather's. He cultivated Jewish opinion, and Acts reports that he executed James the brother of John and imprisoned Peter because this pleased the Jewish leaders (Acts 12:1-3). He died suddenly at Caesarea in AD 44. Acts says an angel struck him because he accepted the crowd's acclaim of him as a god (Acts 12:20-23); Josephus independently describes the same scene, with Agrippa in a robe of silver at games in the theater, the crowd hailing him as divine, and his death of violent abdominal pain five days later (Antiquities 19.343-350).

His son, Agrippa II, was seventeen when his father died, and Claudius judged him too young to rule Judea. He received instead the small kingdom of Chalcis in Lebanon around 50, exchanged it in 53 for Philip's old tetrarchy, and later received parts of Galilee and Perea from Nero. He also held the right to appoint the high priest and oversaw the temple. It is this King Agrippa, with his sister Bernice, who heard Paul's defense before Festus at Caesarea (Acts 25:13 to 26:32) and remarked, “Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?” (Acts 26:28). During the revolt of 66 he tried to restrain his people and then sided with Rome. He died around 92 or 93 according to most modern historians; a report preserved by the ninth-century scholar Photius from Justus of Tiberias puts his death in AD 100. He was the last of the Herodian kings.

The women of the family appear in the New Testament too. Herodias, granddaughter of Herod the Great, married two of her uncles in turn and drove the plot that killed John the Baptist; she followed Antipas into exile. Her daughter, named Salome in Josephus but not in the Gospels, danced before Antipas. Bernice, daughter of Agrippa I, appears beside her brother in Acts 25 and later became the companion of the Roman general and future emperor Titus. Her sister Drusilla left her first husband, the king of Emesa, to marry the Roman governor Felix, and sat with him when Paul spoke to them “about faith in Christ Jesus” (Acts 24:24).

sections.body:
When Archelaus was deposed in AD 6, Judea, Samaria, and Idumea became a Roman province of a minor kind, governed by a man of equestrian rank (the order of Roman gentry below the senators) who answered in some measure to the senatorial legate of the great province of Syria. The governor lived at Caesarea Maritima, on the coast, and came up to Jerusalem with troops at the festivals, when the city was crowded and tense; that is why Pilate was in Jerusalem at Passover. He commanded a few thousand auxiliary soldiers, mostly recruited from the non-Jewish cities of the region, collected the tribute, and held the power of life and death. Day-to-day affairs in Jerusalem were left to the high priest and the council, the Sanhedrin, whose high priests the governors appointed and removed.

The governors before AD 41 bore the title prefect (praefectus), a military title. This was confirmed in 1961, when Italian excavators at Caesarea found a stone reused in the theater that names ‘Pontius Pilatus, prefect of Judea’ and records a building he dedicated to Tiberius. After 44 the governors were called procurators (procurator), a financial title that later writers, including Tacitus, applied back to Pilate as well. The New Testament uses the general Greek word hegemon, ‘governor’, for both.

The province began with a census of property for taxation, conducted by Publius Sulpicius Quirinius, the legate of Syria, in AD 6. It provoked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37), whom Josephus calls the founder of a ‘fourth philosophy’ holding that God alone should be Israel's master. Luke 2:1-2 dates Jesus' birth to a census held “while Quirinius was governor of Syria”, which raises a well-known difficulty, since Jesus was born under Herod, about ten years before Quirinius's census. Some scholars, including Emil Schürer and Raymond E. Brown (The Birth of the Messiah, 1977), conclude that Luke confused the two periods. Others propose that the Greek can mean ‘this census took place before Quirinius was governor’ (a reading defended by Harold Hoehner in Chronological Aspects of the Life of Christ, 1977), or that Quirinius held an earlier command in the region, or that an enrollment begun under Herod was completed later. The question remains open. A similar question attends Acts 5:36, where Gamaliel, speaking in the 30s, mentions a rebel named Theudas before Judas; Josephus places a Theudas under the governor Fadus in the 40s. Some scholars conclude that Luke has misplaced him; others think Gamaliel referred to an earlier Theudas, a common name, whom Josephus does not mention.

sections.body:
Pilate governed Judea for about ten years, from 26 to 36, a long term by the standards of the province. Outside the Gospels he is known from Josephus, from Philo of Alexandria, from Tacitus, from the Caesarea inscription, and from small bronze coins he struck with pagan religious implements on them, a lituus (augur's staff) and a simpulum (libation ladle), symbols that some scholars read as deliberate provocation and others as ordinary Roman imagery.

Josephus tells of several confrontations (Jewish War 2.169-177; Antiquities 18.55-62). Early in his term Pilate brought military standards bearing the emperor's image into Jerusalem by night; a crowd lay before his residence at Caesarea for five days, bared their necks when his soldiers drew swords, and Pilate backed down. Later he used money from the temple treasury to build an aqueduct, and when crowds protested his soldiers beat many to death. Philo (Embassy to Gaius 299-305) reports that Pilate set up gilded shields in Herod's palace in Jerusalem, and that Tiberius ordered them removed after Herod's sons appealed to him; Philo describes Pilate as inflexible and harsh. Luke adds that he had killed Galileans in the temple, “whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices” (Luke 13:1). In 36 his troops attacked a crowd of Samaritans gathered at Mount Gerizim, and after the Samaritans complained, Vitellius, the legate of Syria, sent Pilate to Rome to answer for it. Tiberius died before he arrived, and Pilate disappears from reliable history.

The Gospels show a governor who judged Jesus innocent of sedition but gave way to pressure. Readers have long asked whether this fits the stubborn man of Josephus and Philo. Some historians think the Gospels softened Pilate's guilt as Christians sought peace with Rome. Others, such as Helen Bond (Pontius Pilate in History and Interpretation, 1998), read the Gospel accounts as showing a shrewd governor managing the crowd and the priests for his own ends, which fits the sources better than either a weak or a merely cruel Pilate. The Gospels also give a reason he might yield: the crowd's threat that releasing a claimed king would make him “no friend of Caesar” (John 19:12), a dangerous charge under Tiberius, who punished suspected disloyalty harshly, especially after the fall of his chief minister Sejanus in 31. The Apostles' Creed names Pilate, not to blame him above others, but to fix Jesus' suffering to a real date in human history.

sections.h: Felix, Festus, and the road to war
sections.body:
The procurators after AD 44 governed a province sliding toward revolt, and Acts gives a close view of two of them. Felix, a former slave of the imperial household whose brother Pallas was one of Claudius's most powerful ministers, governed from about 52. Tacitus judged him harshly, as a man who used a king's power with a slave's cruelty and lust. Josephus tells of bandits and of the sicarii (‘dagger-men’) who assassinated opponents in the crowds, including a former high priest, and of an Egyptian prophet who led a crowd to the Mount of Olives promising that Jerusalem's walls would fall; the Roman tribune who arrested Paul took him for that Egyptian (Acts 21:38). Felix kept Paul in custody at Caesarea for two years, hoping for a bribe (Acts 24:26-27).

Festus, who succeeded Felix around 59 or 60, moved quickly on Paul's case, and when he proposed a trial in Jerusalem Paul used his right as a Roman citizen to appeal to the emperor (Acts 25:9-12). Festus died in office in 62. In the gap before Albinus arrived, the high priest Ananus, son of the Annas of the Gospels, convened the Sanhedrin and had James the brother of Jesus and some others stoned. Josephus reports this (Antiquities 20.200), and Agrippa II deposed Ananus for it. Albinus and then Gessius Florus were, in Josephus's account, openly corrupt. In 66 Florus took seventeen talents from the temple treasury and let his soldiers loose on Jerusalem when the people mocked him. The daily sacrifice for the emperor was stopped, and the war began that ended with the temple's destruction in AD 70.

The governors' dates help set the chronology of Paul's life. The Gallio inscription from Delphi dates Gallio's term as proconsul of Achaia, before whom Paul stood in Corinth (Acts 18:12), to about 51 or 52. The change from Felix to Festus, which Acts places two years into Paul's imprisonment, is dated by most scholars to 59 or 60, though proposals range from 55 to 61. Combined, these give the framework for dating Paul's travels and letters.

sections.h: The high priests under Herod and Rome
sections.body:
Before Herod, the high priesthood was hereditary and, under the Hasmoneans, joined to the kingship. Herod broke that pattern. He appointed and deposed high priests at will, choosing men from priestly families of his own choosing, several of them from Egypt and Babylon, so that no high priest could become a rival. The Roman governors continued the practice, and Agrippa II inherited it. In the century before AD 70 there were more than twenty high priests, many of them from a handful of powerful families.

The most powerful of these families was that of Annas (Ananus son of Seth), appointed by Quirinius in AD 6 and removed by Valerius Gratus in 15. Five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him. This explains why Luke can speak of “the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas” (Luke 3:2) as if it were shared, and why John records that Jesus was taken first to Annas (John 18:13): the old man remained the head of the family and the power behind the office. Caiaphas held the post from about 18 to 36 or 37, longer than any other high priest of the Roman period, which suggests he worked well with Pilate; Vitellius removed him shortly after Pilate's recall. In 1990 an ornate ossuary (a bone box) inscribed ‘Joseph son of Caiaphas’ was found in a family tomb in Jerusalem, and many scholars identify it as his, since Josephus gives his full name as Joseph Caiaphas.

Later high priests appear in Acts. Ananias son of Nedebaeus, high priest from about 47 to 59, ordered Paul struck on the mouth at his hearing before the council (Acts 23:2) and came down to Caesarea to accuse him before Felix (Acts 24:1). Josephus remembers him for his greed and says he was killed by rebels at the start of the war in 66.

table.caption: High priests named in the New Testament

sections.body:
Every Herodian ruler and every governor held power at the pleasure of the emperor in Rome, and the New Testament names several of them. Augustus ordered the census of Luke 2:1; Tiberius is the Caesar of Luke 3:1 and of Jesus' answer about the tribute coin (Mark 12:17); Claudius expelled Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2), an event the Roman writer Suetonius also mentions and which is usually dated to 49; and Nero is the Caesar to whom Paul appealed (Acts 25:11). Caligula's attempt in 40 to set up his statue in the Jerusalem temple, abandoned only because of his assassination in January 41, is not mentioned in the New Testament but frightened Jews across the empire and may lie behind the language of Mark 13:14 and 2 Thessalonians 2:4, as some scholars suggest.

The emperors' reigns set the outer frame of the New Testament: Jesus was born under Augustus and crucified under Tiberius; the church spread from Jerusalem into the wider empire under Caligula and Claudius; Paul and, by early tradition, Peter died in Rome under Nero, after the fire of 64; and the temple fell under Vespasian, whose son Titus led the siege.
